Some extreme cases for the first derivative in simulation:

```{r}
excases <- function(no) {
  switch(no,
         dirmix(c(1.2, 7, 4)),
         dirmix(c(1.7, 7, 4)),
         dirmix(c(2, 7, 4)), # mode = c(0.1, 0.6, 0.3); h = 0.1
         dirmix(c(3, 7, 4)),
         dirmix(c(3, 13, 7)), # mode = c(0.1, 0.6, 0.3); h = 0.05
         dirmix(c(6, 31, 16)) # mode = c(0.1, 0.6, 0.3); h = 0.01
         )
}
```

Simulation function:

```{r}
exsimu <- function(mix, seed, n = 500, rep = 5) {
  samp <- DIE_samp(mix, 1e4) # Generate monte Carlo samples
  iae <- ise <- NULL
  for (i in 1:rep) {
    cat(i, " ")
    set.seed(seed[i])
    x <- rdirmix(n, mix)
    fm <- optfm(x)
    fmb <- optfm(x, bound = 1.51)
    
    # ==== Bandwidth from derivative ====
    # Alpha of finite mixture must > 1.5 to ensure L2 integrability of KDE in first derivative
    # c = 1.5
    c <- 1.5
    pih <- optMISEh(fmb$mix, n, 1)
    knpi <- dirkn(x, pih$h, c)
    cvh <- optLSCVh(x, 1)
    kncv <- dirkn(x, cvh$h, c) 
    # c can not be 1.5 in KDE if x contains 0, since alpha = x/h + c should > 1.5
    c <- 1.75
    cvh1 <- optLSCVh(x, 1, c = c)
    kncv1 <- dirkn(x, cvh1$h, c) 
    c <- 2
    cvh2 <- optLSCVh(x, 1, c = c)
    kncv2 <- dirkn(x, cvh2$h, c) 
    
    # ==== Bandwidth from density ====
    pih_den <- optMISEh(fmb$mix, n)
    knpi_den <- dirkn(x, pih_den$h)
    cvh_den <- optLSCVh(x)
    kncv_den <- dirkn(x, cvh_den$h)
    lkh_den  <- optLCVh(x)
    knlk_den <- dirkn(x, lkh_den$h)
    
    IEfm <- DIE(samp, fm$mix)
    IEfmb <- DIE(samp, fmb$mix)
    IEpi <- DIE(samp, knpi)
    IEcv <- DIE(samp, kncv)
    IEcv1 <- DIE(samp, kncv1)
    IEcv2 <- DIE(samp, kncv2)
    IEpi_den <- DIE(samp, knpi_den)
    IEcv_den <- DIE(samp, kncv_den)
    IElk_den <- DIE(samp, knlk_den)
    h <- c(pih$h, cvh$h, cvh1$h, cvh2$h, pih_den$h, cvh_den$h, lkh_den$h)
    viae <- c(seed[i], IEfm$iae, IEfmb$iae, IEpi$iae, IEcv$iae, IEcv1$iae, IEcv2$iae, 
              IEpi_den$iae, IEcv_den$iae, IElk_den$iae)
    vise <- c(seed[i], IEfm$ise, IEfmb$ise, IEpi$ise, IEcv$ise, IEcv1$ise, IEcv2$ise, 
              IEpi_den$ise, IEcv_den$ise, IElk_den$ise)
    iae <- rbind(iae, c(viae, h))
    ise <- rbind(ise, c(vise, h))
  }
  colnames(iae) <- colnames(ise) <- c("seed", "fm", "fm1.5", "PI", "CV", "CV1.75", "CV2", "PI_den", "CV_den", "LK_den",
                                      "PIh", "CVh", "CV1.75h", "CV2h", "PIh_den", "CVh_den", "LKh_den")
  list(iae = iae, ise = ise)
}
```


Some basic setting for simulation:

```{r}
n <- 500
rep <- 5
seed <- ceiling(runif(rep, 1, 1e5))
```

## Model 1: 

Alpha <= 1.5 of the test Dirichlet distribution.

```{r}
mix <- excases(1)
plotdg(mix)
re1 <- exsimu(mix, seed, n, rep)
```

Simulation results:

```{r}
re1
```

When density close to the boundary. It means that our finite mixture's alpha < 1.5.

If we force the finite mixture's alpha > 1.5, the estimation of the finite mixture will be bad. (fm1.5 >> fm)

Since Plug-in method highly depends on fm1.5, its results also bad, and its bandwidth close to 1 (why?).

CV method is not rely on finite mixture. It is better than PI, but compared with other results, CV is still bad. And as c increases, the results getting worse. 

Density based PI and CV selectors are even better than derivative-based ones.


## Model 3:

Alpha = 1.7 of the test Dirichlet distribution.

```{r}
mix <- excases(2)
plotdg(mix)
re2 <- exsimu(mix, seed, n, rep)
```

Simulation results:

```{r}
lapply(re2, function(i) i[, !colnames(i) %in% c("CV1.75", "CV2", "CV1.75h", "CV2h")])
```

Since alpha > 1.5 for the test model, the alpha of finite mixture estimation will not outside the boundary, thus the results of fm and fm1.5 is the same.

Density based PI and CV selectors still better than derivative-based ones, but the differences get narrowed.

## Model 3:

Alpha = 2 of the test Dirichlet distribution.

```{r}
mix <- excases(3)
plotdg(mix)
re3 <- exsimu(mix, seed, n, rep)
```

```{r}
lapply(re3, function(i) i[, !colnames(i) %in% c("fm1.5", "CV1.75", "CV2", "CV1.75h", "CV2h")])
```

Density based PI and CV selectors perform similar to derivative-based ones now.

## Model 4:

Alpha = 3 of the test Dirichlet distribution.

```{r}
mix <- excases(4)
plotdg(mix)
re4 <- exsimu(mix, seed, n, rep)
```

```{r}
lapply(re4, function(i) i[, !colnames(i) %in% c("fm1.5", "CV1.75", "CV2", "CV1.75h", "CV2h")])
```

In this case, derivative-based PI and CV selectors are better, just worse than fm.

## Model 5:

Mode is the same as model 3, but alpha_0 is larger.

```{r}
mix <- excases(5)
plotdg(mix)
re5 <- exsimu(mix, seed, n, rep)
```

```{r}
lapply(re5, function(i) i[, !colnames(i) %in% c("fm1.5", "CV1.75", "CV2", "CV1.75h", "CV2h")])
```

## Model 6:

Mode is the same as model 3, but alpha_0 is larger.

```{r}
mix <- excases(6)
plotdg(mix)
re6 <- exsimu(mix, seed, n, rep)
```

```{r}
lapply(re6, function(i) i[, !colnames(i) %in% c("fm1.5", "CV1.75", "CV2", "CV1.75h", "CV2h")])
```
